candidates.statement: Supreme Court has explained that the language “accompanying such article” in the labeling definition is interpreted broadly to include materials that supplement, explain, or are otherwise textually related to the article. No physical attachment between the materials and the article is necessary; rather, “it is the textual relationship between the items that is significant.” Kordel v. United States , 355 U.S. 345, 350 (1948). In evaluating whether materials “accompany” a product, Kordel also considered whether the drug product and the materials related to the drug product were part of an integrated distribution program (Ibid., 348). In United States v . Urbuteit , which was decided on the same day as Kordel , the U.S. Supreme Court further explained that, in making a labeling determination, a court should review the “transaction in its entirety” to determine whether the product distribution and literature were “functional[ly] . . . integrated.” 335 U.S. 355, 357-58 (1948).

candidates.statement: Generally, the recommendations provided in this guidance are intended to align with ongoing Agency initiatives across all product centers, including digital health initiatives at the Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH). 13 In developing this guidance, the Agency has considered existing Agency policies for the regulation of software to ensure consistent regulation of device software and efficient, coordinated review in instances when prescription drug use- related software is reviewed by the Agency as a device. This guidance does not alter the statutory or regulatory framework for devices or the applicability of such framework to prescription drug use-related software. Rather, it focuses on the application of drug labeling authorities to the end-user output of prescription drug use-related software, regardless of whether the software is regulated as a device under the FD&C Act. In addition, this guidance does not take a position on the types of software functions that a sponsor may propose to include in prescription drug use-related software. 14 While the end-user output of a software function is subject to FDA drug labeling authorities, some software functions may meet the definition of device 15 in the FD&C Act and would be subject to device requirements. Determining whether a software function meets the definition of device in the FD&C Act is outside the scope of this guidance. In the case of a software function that also meets the device definition, please refer to applicable CDRH policies 18 , as this guidance solely addresses the drug labeling associated with claims regarding the use of such software

candidates.statement: For prescription drug products and prescription CDER-led or CBER-led, drug-device combination products, FDA-required labeling is the labeling that is reviewed and approved by FDA as part of an NDA, ANDA, or BLA, as well as supplemental applications (21 CFR 314.50(c)(2) and 314.94(a)(8); 21 CFR 601.2(a)). The PI is part of the FDA-required labeling and must contain a summary of the essential scientific information needed for the safe and effective use of the drug. 18 Additionally, the PI must be informative, accurate, up to date, and neither promotional in tone nor false or misleading in any particular. 19 , 20 Promotional labeling is generally any labeling other than the FDA-required labeling.
candidates.context: II. BACKGROUND FDA recognizes that the use of software with prescription drugs has the potential to offer new opportunities for patient care, and the Agency is working to promote responsible, risk-based oversight of such software. Various software functions, including those associated with mobile applications (mobile apps 17 ) or webpages, may have a variety of health-related uses, such as assisting patients with tracking their own drug administration, providing individualized dosing recommendations, predicting treatment response, and managing side effects. To the extent that sponsors of drug products or combination products disseminate software for use with one or more of their products, FDA intends to implement its policies and exercise its authorities, including drug labeling authorities, according to an evidence-driven, risk-based framework. candidates.statement: III. PRESCRIPTION DRUG USE-RELATED SOFTWARE AND END-USER OUTPUT As mentioned in the Introduction, prescription drug use-related software generally includes software that (1) is disseminated by or on behalf of a drug sponsor and (2) produces an end-user output that supplements, explains, or is otherwise textually related to one or more of the sponsor’s drug products, regardless of whether the software is regulated as a device under the FD&C Act. When a sponsor proposes to disseminate prescription drug use-related software for use with a drug product, FDA intends to analyze several factors to determine whether the end- user output should be treated as FDA-required labeling or promotional labeling and how, or if, the corresponding software function should be described in the PI. These factors include (1) whether the prescription drug use-related software is essential to the safe and effective use of the product, (2) whether FDA determines based on evidence provided by the sponsor that there is a meaningful improvement in a clinical outcome (see section IV.A of this guidance) when the prescription drug use-related software is used with the drug, and (3) whether the prescription drug use-related software relies on data from a device or device constituent part.

candidates.statement: Typically, the PI should describe device-connected software functions (e.g., in the HOW SUPPLIED/STORAGE AND HANDLING section). However, which section(s) of the PI include(s) this information should be determined on a case-by-case basis, depending on the specific software function and end-user output generated by the prescription drug use-related software. For example, if FDA determines based on evidence provided by a sponsor that use of the prescription drug use-related software (device-connected or standalone software function) results in a meaningful improvement in a clinical outcome (e.g., compared to drug product use without the prescription drug use-related software), it might be appropriate to include such information in the CLINICAL STUDIES section of the PI.

candidates.statement: Notably, in these examples, the prescription drug use-related software relies on data directly transferred from the device constituent part of the combination product. The information in the PI can be used by the prescriber to inform the patient that such information is transferred to a mobile app during their use of the product and that use of the software is optional. The presence of this information in the PI also may help to differentiate between a combination product with and without device-connected software functions. In these examples, the PI (e.g., in the HOW SUPPLIED/STORAGE AND HANDLING section) should provide a brief description of the device constituent part and the associated software function(s) (see Appendix B for an example), while the end-user output itself would be considered promotional labeling. In these examples, information beyond describing the device constituent part and associated software function(s) should not be included in the PI. In general, regardless of whether the sponsor has submitted evidence of a meaningful improvement in a clinical outcome, FDA recommends that when the prescription drug use-related software is not considered necessary for the safe and effective use of the drug product, the sponsor should include a statement in the PI where the software function and device constituent part are described noting that use of the software is not necessary for the safe and effective use of the product.

candidates.statement: “… For each injection, AUTOINJECTOR-XYZ can record the dose of DRUG-X injected and the time of the injection. Such data may be transferred using Bluetooth wireless technology to a mobile app and subsequently to a cloud-based web application for patient or health care practitioner use. Use of the associated mobile app is not necessary for safe and effective use of DRUG-X.” (Include other required information in the HOW SUPPLIED/STORAGE AND HANDLING section (21 CFR 201.57(c)(17)).) The end-user output includes any material (content) presented on the mobile app and on the web application to the end user. The end-user output would be considered promotional labeling and should be submitted on Form FDA 2253 at the time of initial dissemination.
candidates.context: The product in Example 1 is reviewed under a biologics license application (BLA). The Center for Devices and Radiological Health may be consulted, as appropriate. Under this situation, FDA would generally recommend including the following or similar statement in the HOW SUPPLIED/STORAGE AND HANDLING section of the PI: APPENDIX C: EXAMPLE OF DESCRIBING THE STANDALONE PRESCRIPTION DRUG USE-RELATED SOFTWARE FUNCTION(S) IN THE PRESCRIBING INFORMATION WHEN FDA DETERMINES THERE IS EVIDENCE DEMONSTRATING A MEANINGFUL IMPROVEMENT IN A CLINICAL OUTCOME The example below is for illustrative purposes only and shows how a sponsor might describe standalone software functions in the CLINICAL STUDIES section of the PI when FDA determines there is evidence from adequate and well-controlled studies that demonstrates a meaningful improvement in a clinical outcome associated with the use of the prescriptio

candidates.statement: The DRUG-Y with the mobile app group demonstrated a statistically significant greater reduction in HbA1c compared to the DRUG-Y alone group (mean difference: -0.X%, 95% CI: -X.X to -X.X).” ( Include other required information in the CLINICAL STUDIES section.) 38 The end-user output would be considered FDA-required labeling. Certain postapproval changes to the end-user output should be reviewed and approved by FDA (see section IV.A of this guidance).
